title: The Difference Between Hope and Optimism
author: Arthur C. Brooks
summary: Arthur Brooks opens his weekly newsletter with a comic memory of his father, who catastrophized about running out of gas on every drive over the Cascades yet was somehow pessimistic and hopeful at once. He uses that paradox to distinguish two concepts often treated as synonyms. Citing a 2004 study in the Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, he explains that optimism is the belief that things will turn out well, while hope is the conviction that one can act to make things better. Drawing on Teresa of Avila's view that hope comes from will and commitment, he offers three steps for building it: imagine a specific better future, envision yourself acting, and then act at the person-to-person level. He ends with Mother Teresa's counsel to do small things with great love.
points: Brooks's father imagined the worst to avoid disappointment, showing that pessimism and hope can coexist.
Research distinguishes hope, focused on attaining personal goals, from optimism, a general expectation of good outcomes.
Hope is framed as a matter of will and commitment rather than temperament, following Teresa of Avila.
Building hope means detailing a concrete better future, imagining realistic personal action, and then following through on small acts.
quotes: Years later, I asked him why he did this. He thought about it, and told me he preferred to be pleasantly surprised rather than bitterly disappointed, so he imagined the worst. In a strange way, my dad was pessimistic but hopeful at the same time.
People tend to use hope and optimism as synonyms, but that isn’t accurate.
Optimism is the belief that things will turn out well; hope makes no such assumption but is a conviction that one can act to make things better.
The Catholic nun and mystic Teresa of Ávila believed that hope comes from will and commitment.

Rather than basking in the glow of a fictitious city and leaving it at that, make a list of the specific elements that will have improved; for instance, more affordable housing, better public policy and regulation, or more attention to substance abuse and mental-health needs.
Avoid illusions of being the invincible savior; instead, imagine helping one real person, convincing one policymaker, or increasing the compassion of one fellow citizen.
Your specific action might feel like an exercise in futility, because it is so small. This is the voice of hopelessness inside your head.
